evidence: The constructor receives OrderRepository, ProductRepository, IdGenerator and Clock as interfaces defined in the domain layer. The service uses these ports and never reaches into infrastructure directly.

placeOrder hands the stock rules to the domain (product.canReserve, product.reserve) and builds the order with new Order(...). The service only coordinates the two-phase check-then-reserve across both aggregates.
changeState and cancel call order.transitionTo to enforce the state machine, and product.ship and product.release to change stock. The service only decides which aggregates take part.
The file contains no HTTP, database, framework or serialization code. Transport lives in src/infrastructure/http.ts and src/infrastructure/server.ts, which import this service.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrderService is a standard application-layer use-case service. Its work is orchestration: it validates the incoming command, loads aggregates through repository ports, delegates the actual rules to domain objects, saves state through the ports and returns snapshots. Domain objects own the business rules: Product.canReserve, reserve, ship and release; Order.transitionTo and nextState; and the assertPositiveInteger helper. The file itself has no persistence, transport or framework logic: no SQL, no HTTP and no serialization beyond domain snapshots. Some logic does sit in the service: merging duplicate product lines, checking that stock is available for the whole order before reserving any of it, and tying stock changes to the shipped and cancelled transitions. All of this coordinates two aggregates (Order and Product) inside one use case, which is what an application service is for. The 'at least one item' check could arguably live in the Order constructor, but it reads as validation of the incoming command, not a misplaced responsibility.
